title: Holy Thursday
hookLine: the washing of feet, the new commandment, and the watch at the altar of repose

cards: In English the day is sometimes called Maundy Thursday, an odd word that hides its meaning. In Britain the monarch gives out special coins that day.

In parish churches something stranger happens: after the homily, the priest takes off his outer vestment, ties a towel around his waist, kneels on the floor, and washes the feet of people chosen from the congregation.
The odd English word and the odd ritual come from the same Latin word.

teach.b: Holy Thursday evening begins the Triduum, the three great days. The Mass of the Lord's Supper remembers the night Jesus gave his disciples the Eucharist, and the gospel is John 13.

During supper, Jesus gets up, lays aside his garments, takes a towel, pours water into a basin, and washes his disciples' feet, a job usually left to servants. Peter protests: you will never wash my feet.
Jesus says, if I don't wash you, you have no part with me. Then he sits back down and explains: if I, your Lord and master, have washed your feet, you ought to wash one another's.
And a little later, the command: "A new commandment I give unto you: That you love one another, as I have loved you."
In Latin, commandment is mandatum, and from mandatum comes maundy. So the rite of foot washing is called the Mandatum.
The Gloria is sung tonight with the bells ringing, and then the bells fall silent until the Easter Vigil.

teach.h: THE WATCH AT THE ALTAR OF REPOSE.
teach.b: After communion, the remaining consecrated hosts are carried in procession to a side altar, the altar of repose, decked with flowers and candles. The main altar is stripped bare. And people stay.

teach.h: LOVE ONE ANOTHER, AS I HAVE LOVED YOU.
teach.b: They keep watch, often until midnight, remembering Gethsemane, where Jesus asked his friends to stay awake while he prayed in anguish, and found them sleeping.
In the Douay-Rheims: "What? Could you not watch one hour with me?" On this night, some Catholics walk from church to church, visiting several altars of repose, keeping company with him in each.

how: At the Evening Mass of the Lord's Supper on Holy Thursday, the priest may wash the feet of members of the congregation, the Eucharist is carried to an altar of repose, the main altar is stripped, and the faithful keep watch, often until midnight.

s: maundy comes from the Latin for commandment
mandatum, from 'a new commandment I give unto you'.
the church bells ring all through the Triduum
they ring at the Gloria tonight, then fall silent until the Easter Vigil.
washing feet was ordinary work for a host's servants
which is why Peter protests when Jesus does it.

games.q: you're Peter at supper. your teacher has taken off his outer garment, tied on a towel, and knelt in front of you with a basin. what do you say?
o: you will never wash my feet.
games.why: Peter refuses, until Jesus says, if I wash thee not, thou shalt have no part with me. then Peter asks him to wash his hands and head too.

practice: On this night people keep watch at the altar of repose, and an hour is the old measure; for now, sit wherever you are and keep company.

Picture the garden, olive trees, the dark, friends asleep, one man praying, and stay awake with him. If you pray, simply stay, no words needed; if you don't, keep watch for someone you know who is suffering tonight.

wordCard.voice: Mandatum. Latin for commandment: the new commandment to love one another, the foot washing named for it, and the root of maundy. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: commandment, from 'mandatum novum do vobis', John 13:34 in the Vulgate.

carryVoice: Your line: love one another. The towel and the basin show what that looks like. That's day six hundred sixty.
